strengths: Addresses two genuinely under-explored perceptual criteria in UV parameterization—semantic coherence and seam visibility—that prior automatic methods largely ignore, and combines them within a single differentiable framework.

The technical pipeline is coherent and well described: a bi-directional cycle-mapping backbone for geometry-preserving parameterization, a ShDF+graph-cut based semantic partitioning scheme, a differentiable soft seam-extraction procedure, and an ambient-occlusion-weighted seam loss that is fully justified and mathematically detailed.

Reasonably thorough qualitative results across a variety of meshes (simple primitives to more complex articulated/mechanical objects), and clear visual evidence (checkerboard texturing, AO histograms) that the visibility-aware objective shifts seams toward occluded regions.

Useful ablations isolating the effect of the partitioning strategy (ShDF vs. SAMesh) and of the semantic/visibility losses on geometric distortion metrics, showing the added objectives do not substantially harm conformality/equiareality.
Good reproducibility effort: detailed appendix on the ShDF partitioning algorithm, network architecture (layer-wise Table 3), and loss formulations.
weaknesses: Quantitative evaluation is conducted on only a handful of individual meshes (Rabbit, Cow, Fish, Duckie, etc.) rather than a larger benchmark dataset (e.g., ShapeNet, Thingi10k, ABC), making it unclear how well the reported metrics generalize and whether differences are statistically meaningful (no variance/error bars reported).

The semantic-awareness quantitative metric (Hamming distance/Rand Index) uses SAMesh output as a pseudo-ground-truth, which is questionable since SAMesh is itself an unsupervised heuristic segmentation baseline also used elsewhere in the paper (including in the ablation as an alternative partitioner)—this creates a somewhat circular evaluation without true semantic ground truth or human annotation.

The visibility metric (mean seam AO) is essentially the same quantity the visibility loss directly optimizes, so strong performance on this metric is close to tautological; a more convincing evaluation would use an independent rendering-based seam-artifact measure across multiple lighting/viewpoints or a human perceptual study, which is absent.

No comparison against several directly relevant semantic-aware or visibility-aware baselines explicitly discussed in related work (e.g., Vermandere et al. 2024, Mukherjee et al. 2024, Seamster, GraphSeam, Weill-Duflos et al. 2023)—comparisons are limited mostly to FlexPara, OptCuts, and generic industry tools.

The method appears to require per-mesh (test-time) optimization of the backbone and per-part networks (Algorithm 1 shows a training loop per mesh), which is in tension with the title's framing as "representation learning"; scalability/generalization to unseen shapes without retraining and total end-to-end optimization cost per mesh are not clearly discussed.

Limited discussion of failure cases, computational cost/scalability trade-offs of the per-part partition-and-parameterize approach (including UV-space utilization losses from the simple grid-based atlas packer), and sensitivity to hyperparameters (K, τ_scale, β, γ, λ_vis) is largely absent from the main text.

strengths: Addresses a genuine practical bottleneck (manual UV parameterization) with a well-motivated combination of two under-explored perceptual objectives: semantic alignment and visibility-aware seam placement.

The overall pipeline is unsupervised and differentiable, built on an existing geometry-preserving backbone, with clear per-module loss design (semantic partition + per-part parameterization + atlas packing; AO-weighted differentiable seam detection).

Extensive empirical evaluation: qualitative comparisons across multiple meshes/viewpoints, quantitative metrics (Hamming distance, Rand Index, mean seam AO, conformality, equiareality), and a fairly large user study (115 participants split into expert/general groups) showing strong preference for the proposed method.

Thorough ablation studies (segmentation backbone choice: ShDF vs. SAMesh vs. PartField; UV packing strategies; visibility loss on/off; combined vs. individual objective pipelines) and an honest discussion of trade-offs between geometry-preservation and semantic/visibility objectives.
Good reproducibility effort: detailed appendix with architecture/layer tables, algorithmic pseudocode, loss definitions, and transparent disclosure of LLM usage for writing.
weaknesses: The two most directly related prior works explicitly cited as tackling the same problems individually (Vermandere et al. 2024 for semantic-aware UV mapping, Weill-Duflos et al. 2023 / Sheffer & Hart 2002 / Ray et al. 2010 for visibility/seam-aware placement) are never used as empirical baselines; comparisons are instead limited to generic parameterization tools (FlexPara, OptCuts, Maya, Blender, xatlas) that do not target these objectives, making the central novelty claim ("first to jointly address both") harder to substantiate quantitatively against the closest competitors.

The core geometry-preserving backbone is explicitly non-novel (reused from Zhao et al. 2025/FlexPara); the semantic partitioning relies on a classical hand-crafted algorithm (Shapira et al. 2008 ShDF + GMM + graph cuts) rather than a learned method, so the technical novelty is largely confined to the loss formulations that connect these existing components, which is a comparatively incremental contribution.

The visibility-aware pipeline incurs a drastic training-time overhead (roughly 20-30x slower than the FlexPara baseline per Table 9), with only speculative future-work mitigations (parallelization, spatial hashing) proposed rather than demonstrated, raising practical scalability concerns.

Method requires per-mesh optimization (no amortized/generalizable model), and all demonstrated meshes are small-to-moderate single objects (rabbit, cow, duckie, etc.) rather than a standard large-scale 3D benchmark (e.g., ShapeNet/Objaverse), limiting evidence of generality and production-scale applicability.

The semantic-awareness quantitative metric (Hamming distance/Rand Index) uses SAMesh outputs as a proxy "ground truth," which is itself an automatic, imperfect segmentation method, raising concerns about circularity/validity of this evaluation.

Reported gains are occasionally marginal or come with trade-offs (e.g., Table 7 shows only slight conformality improvements and reduced equiareality for the combined pipeline; Table 3 Hamming distance improvement over baselines is moderate), while user-study preference numbers are extremely lopsided (e.g., 91-93% preference) without reported inter-rater agreement or statistical significance testing, which could reflect an easy/binary comparison design rather than robust superiority.

The ablation on segmentation strategy (Table 6, Figs. 14-15) shows PartField often producing qualitatively better semantic segmentations than the adopted default (ShDF), and the paper acknowledges no clear causal link between segmentation quality and final UV geometry metrics, somewhat undermining confidence in the specific design choice used for the main results.
